captions: The diagram introduces key architectural conventions, including average aggregation, depthwise convolutions, and trainable scaling parameters.
In the Swin-Transformer block, input features pass through layer normalization alongside an initial residual shortcut.
Normalized features enter the window and shifted-window multi-head self-attention module to capture spatial context.
The attention outputs are then merged with the initial residual connection.
The first Mona adapter layer processes the aggregated representation to enhance visual feature adaptation.
Features undergo a second layer normalization step before the feed-forward network, accompanied by another skip connection.
A feed-forward layer then transforms the intermediate token representations.
The feed-forward output is summed with its corresponding shortcut.
A second Mona layer further refines the features before outputting the final representation of the Swin-Transformer block.
Inside the Mona layer, input features undergo layer normalization scaled by a trainable factor, while a parallel skip branch is scaled by a second factor.
The scaled feature streams are combined at an addition node to regulate input distribution.
A down projection layer reduces channel dimensionality before branching into multi-scale convolutional paths and residual shortcuts.
Three parallel depthwise convolutions with 3x3, 5x5, and 7x7 kernels extract multi-scale visual patterns.
Outputs from all three kernel branches are combined using an averaging operation.
The averaged depthwise feature is added to the pre-convolution residual branch.
A 1x1 convolution aggregates point-wise channel features alongside an adjacent residual shortcut.
The 1x1 convolution output is summed with its shortcut connection.
A GeLU activation function introduces non-linearity.
An up projection layer restores the original feature channel dimensions.
Finally, the outer residual is added to yield the complete output of the Mona layer.
Finally, the blend operation generates the synthesized target view.
This diagram outlines the architecture of the GLASS framework.
Processing begins with an input image routed directly into the Encoder.
The frozen Encoder branches into the Slot Attention Module and Instance Guidance.
Both the active Slot Attention Module and Instance Guidance feed into the Slots representations.
The Slots are then forwarded to the Decoder.
The frozen Decoder generates the output while connecting to Semantic Guidance.
Semantic Guidance feeds back into the Slots, producing the final output image.
In the portrait attributes subspace modeling stage, the pipeline begins by receiving a reference portrait image and driving video frames.
A frozen DECA network decomposes the video frames into three-dimensional facial attributes, extracting lighting, pose, and shape parameters.
These parameters are rendered into three-dimensional shading hints and passed through a trainable shading adapter to extract extrinsic shading features.
Simultaneously, the reference image is processed by a reference adapter to extract intrinsic identity features, which are randomly combined with shading features.
In parallel, a frozen VAE encoder projects the input video frames into noisy latent representations.
The masked reference portrait is encoded and concatenated with noisy latents, while a CLIP encoder provides global semantic conditioning.
These inputs feed into Stable Video Diffusion, passing through convolutional, self-attention, cross-attention, and temporal-attention blocks.
The denoised latent representation is then decoded by the VAE decoder into reconstructed video frames.
In the relighting and animation stage, the system ingests target lighting alongside driving video frames, a reference portrait, and mask inputs.
DECA extracts target lighting coefficients, motion pose from the driving video, and facial shape geometry from the reference portrait.
A motion alignment module aligns pose and shape to render target shading hints for the shading adapter, paired with the reference adapter.
A multi-condition classifier-free guidance module constructs combined condition sets from both adapter outputs.
Reference identity latents and semantic CLIP embeddings are processed and formatted for diffusion model injection.
Stable Video Diffusion leverages multi-condition guidance to modulate lighting strength while preserving identity consistency.
Finally, the VAE decoder outputs the final animated portrait video frames with accurate lighting control and seamless motion transfer.
The pipeline begins with two input sequences tracked over time: camera image frames and pressure sensor maps.
Each input stream is processed by a dedicated Encoder module.
The encoded features then pass through respective modules labeled LSAM.
Both feature streams feed into the Fusion Cross-Attention Module, designated as FCAM.
The combined representations are forwarded into the Regressor block.
The Regressor estimates pose and translation parameters, governed by pose and translation loss functions.
These parameters produce three-dimensional joint positions, supervised by three-dimensional and contact losses.
The joint positions pass through Orthographic Projection under a two-dimensional loss.
This yields a sequence of full three-dimensional human poses over time along with contact region visualizations.
The bottom panel details the architecture of the Fusion Cross-Attention Module alongside an operation legend.
Processing begins with incoming Image Feature and Pressure Feature blocks.
The Image Feature branches into Image Value and Image Key, while the Pressure Feature produces a Pressure Query.
The Image Key and Pressure Query undergo matrix multiplication, followed by a SoftMax operation.
The resulting weights are multiplied with the Image Value, then added to a skip connection from the Image Feature.
This combined signal enters the Position-wise Feed-Forward block.
Finally, the feed-forward output is concatenated with a skip connection from the Pressure Feature to yield the module output.
The pipeline begins in Section A with Hierarchical Blocks, taking an initial descriptive text prompt for analysis.
The prompt is analyzed to determine the optimization order based on occlusion hierarchy.
Block one targets more occluded items first, beginning with a coarse base human avatar.
It then performs precise optimization on the yellow shirt.
Next, optimization proceeds to the pink trousers, linking into the detailed part-optimization workflow.
Finally, the blue leather shoes are refined to complete Block one.
In Section B, Part-Segmentation isolates the trousers using two-dimensional segment probabilities.
The segmented part is isolated and passed to fine-grained optimization guided by the text prompt.
SDS loss is applied to produce the avatar with precisely rendered pink trousers.
The automatic pipeline extends across sequential blocks toward less occluded layers.
In Block n b, the outermost black coat is added coarsely and then refined to a precise state.
Section C outlines Gaussian Extension, where new Gaussian kernels are densified for adding a coat.
The densified avatar is optimized using SDS loss and passed into Label Elimination to remove redundant kernels.
This results in a clean avatar model with the extended garment layer.
Section D breaks down Label Elimination, starting from original Gaussian kernels and densifying new ones.
SAM is applied to segment part semantics and assign labels to the Gaussian kernels.
Redundant newly added kernels that do not belong to the new part are eliminated.
Only the original and segment Gaussian kernels are retained in the final structure.
The model begins by projecting the input tokens into continuous representations via the input embedding layer.
In parallel, structure-oriented vector quantization clusters these embeddings into discrete classes of structurally equivalent entities.
Both streams are then processed across multiple stacked Transformer layers.
In the standard embedding stream on the left, the representations first pass through layer normalization.
Value, key, and query vectors are projected from the normalized output.
These vectors are processed by multi-head attention and combined with the input via a residual connection.
A residual feed-forward network then produces the layer representation for the standard stream.
Simultaneously, the quantized branch is fed into its own layer normalization block.
It generates corresponding value, key, and query projections based on the structurally quantized features.
These are passed through multi-head attention and integrated through a residual addition.
The residual feed-forward network on the right then outputs the structure-oriented layer representation.
Finally, the objective minimizes the difference between the standard and quantized stream representations, regularizing the model to induce systematic attention patterns.
To begin, input egocentric video frames are fed into a frozen video transformer backbone.
The visual encoder extracts spatio-temporal feature maps representing the video sequence.
In parallel, narration sentences and extracted noun phrases pass through a frozen text backbone.
This yields a global sentence embedding along with fine-grained noun embeddings.
A set of learnable queries is defined, consisting of hand queries, object queries, and a global video query.
The object-aware decoder uses cross-attention to allow these queries to attend to the visual feature map.
The decoder produces localized summary vectors for hands and objects, as well as a video-level embedding.
During training, auxiliary box and semantic heads predict spatial bounding boxes and semantic object classes from the summary vectors.
Finally, the model is trained jointly with bounding box loss, cross-modal video-text contrastive loss, and word-level grounding loss.
The framework begins with an input portrait image.
A geometry-aware encoder projects the input image into the latent space.
This yields an extended latent code representing coarse geometry and appearance.
The latent code is passed into a pre-trained generator, extracting intermediate feature maps while building a 3D tri-plane representation.
The resulting tri-plane encapsulates the canonical 3D volume synthesized from the latent code.
A neural rendering decoder then renders the volume under the estimated camera pose.
This produces an initial coarse reconstruction of the input face.
Next, the framework computes an image residual between the input and its initial reconstruction, pairing it with the generator feature maps.
The Adaptive Feature Alignment module aligns these residual features into the canonical space using cross-attention.
This produces refined latent feature maps containing restored fine-grained textural details.
These modified features are then forwarded through the remaining generator layers.
This constructs a refined tri-plane while identifying visible and occluded 3D point sets based on the input view.
An occlusion-aware fusion combines the visible refined details with the base tri-plane to prevent distortion in unobserved regions.
The mixed tri-plane is then supplied to the neural rendering decoder under the target camera pose.
Finally, the system renders the high-fidelity inversion image with precise identity details and 3D consistency.

In the first stage, the framework begins with a sparse set of casually captured input images of the subject.
These images are used to train a Partial DreamBooth model, personalizing a diffusion model while mitigating viewpoint overfitting.
An initial neural radiance field is initialized and rendered across various camera viewpoints.
Score Distillation Sampling loss from the Partial DreamBooth model guides the optimization of this initial NeRF asset.
In stage two, multi-view images are rendered along random camera viewpoints from the initial NeRF representation.
These rendered perspectives are passed through an image-to-image translation process using a fully-trained DreamBooth model.
This produces pseudo multi-view subject images that improve subject likeness while strictly preserving viewpoint poses.
In stage three, the pseudo multi-view images are used to further fine-tune the model into a Multi-view DreamBooth.
A final NeRF asset is initialized to reconstruct the complete three-dimensional geometry and appearance.
A multi-view reconstruction loss enforces direct pixel fidelity against the generated pseudo multi-view targets.
Concurrently, Score Distillation Sampling loss from the Multi-view DreamBooth refines novel views, producing the finalized 3D asset.
The framework begins with Stage 1, generating 2D-to-3D proposals directly from a single monocular input image.
An off-the-shelf monocular 3D object detector extracts initial features and coarse bounding box estimates.
These predicted 3D bounding boxes establish bottom-up anchors across the scene.
Next, a top-down sampling strategy generates a dense set of proposals around the anchors within a local 3D grid.
Stage 2 performs 3D-to-2D proposal verification to accurately refine and denoise the generated proposals.
Each 3D bounding box proposal is parameterized by its 3D shape, projected 2D corner and center points, and 2D bounding box corners.
In the proposal embedding step, these elements are converted into geometric encodings, projection point appearance encodings, and region-of-interest appearance encodings.
Under intra-proposal attention, a Perceiver module performs cross-attention using the point appearance features as queries and geometric features as keys and values.
After self-attention, the resulting geometry-aware point features serve as keys and values for a second cross-attention stage queried by region-of-interest appearance features.
An inter-proposal self-attention block then models interactions across all proposals to output category classification scores and 3D shape residuals.
This produces the final, highly accurate 3D bounding box detections.
The framework begins with an input pose sequence comprising sparsely sampled keyframes alongside interpolated frames.
These poses are mapped into the embedding space through a pose embedding layer with linear projection.
This produces a sequence of projected embedding tokens representing the frames.
The tokens are then fed into a stack of stacked MixSynthEncoder blocks.
A top linear projection layer transforms the refined embedding features back into the pose dimension.
This outputs the refined and fully recovered human pose sequence across the video.
Looking inside the MixSynthEncoder, standard multi-head self-attention is replaced with MixSynth Attention.
The input first enters the MixSynth Attention module to synthesize spatial and temporal relations concurrently.
The attended features pass through a residual connection followed by layer normalization.
The normalized representations are then processed by a point-wise feed-forward network.
A second residual connection and layer normalization complete the encoder block.
Within the synthetic attention operation, the input splits into two parallel branches.
The input features are arranged into temporal slices and transposed spatial slices.
Linear layers independently generate temporal and spatial synthetic attention matrices to model inter-frame and inter-joint importance.
The generated attention weights modulate the feature representations alongside skip connections.
Finally, the temporal and spatial branches are summed and fused by a linear layer to produce the output.
The framework begins by collecting diverse multi-vehicle perspectives and driving scenes across different environments.
A physically based rendering engine manages the three-dimensional vehicle models, surrounding scenes, base textures, and camera parameters.
This rendering process generates a reference image, a vehicle silhouette mask, and a corresponding depth map.
An adversarial texture patch is parameterized alongside projection augmentations and camera parameters.
Triplanar mapping projects the adversarial texture onto the vehicle surface using depth and camera geometry.
Masking operations then separate the background, isolating both the masked reference vehicle and the projected texture.
The Neural Texture Renderer fuses these inputs to synthesize a realistically textured vehicle while preserving physical lighting characteristics.
The adversarial vehicle is composited back onto the background scene to produce the complete adversarial image.
A random output augmentation module applies digital transformations, such as scaling and shifting, to enhance texture robustness.
The augmented image is then fed into the target vehicle detector, measuring the degradation in detection confidence.
In parallel, a camouflage function extracts dominant background colors to promote natural visual blending.
Camouflage, smoothness, and detection attack losses are aggregated into a total loss and backpropagated to optimize the adversarial texture.
During evaluation, the optimized world-aligned adversarial texture is applied to target three-dimensional vehicles inside Unreal Engine.
Finally, the rendered scenes undergo physical simulation to evaluate evasion performance against state-of-the-art vehicle detectors.
The framework reconstructs articulated objects across multiple distinct states.
The first input state captures the object in its closed configuration.
An intermediate canonical state is defined to balance supervision across input configurations.
The second input state presents the object in an open configuration.
In the optimization loop, neural radiance fields and motion parameters are jointly refined.
For an active input state, camera rays define points and viewing directions.
A learned transformation function maps these query rays into the canonical space.
This establishes ray sample coordinates in the canonical frame.
The static field queries the original ray samples to output density and color for immovable parts.
Concurrently, the mobile field queries canonical samples to determine density and appearance for movable parts.
Composite volume rendering integrates contributions from both fields along each ray.
This integration produces synthesized images corresponding to each articulation state.
Finally, a photometric loss compares the rendered images with ground-truth views to supervise the entire framework.
The framework takes as input the RGB image alongside a concatenated map of user prompt clicks and the previous segmentation mask.
Two symmetric patch embedding layers independently project the input image and the click maps into token sequences of matching dimensions.
These token embeddings are merged through element-wise addition before being forwarded into the network.
The merged tokens are processed by a plain Vision Transformer backbone, which maintains single-scale representations across stacked transformer blocks.
From the backbone's final feature map, a convolutional neck generates a multi-scale simple feature pyramid across four spatial resolutions.
All four pyramid levels are then fed concurrently into the lightweight MLP segmentation head.
Inside the head, features are projected by an initial MLP layer, upsampled and concatenated, and then passed through another MLP layer and sigmoid activation.
This produces a single-channel intermediate feature map at quarter resolution.
An upsampling step restores the resolution to the full image dimensions, yielding the predicted segmentation mask.
Finally, the predicted segmentation is compared with the ground truth mask to compute the loss and supervise training.
The framework takes a two-dimensional training image alongside positive and negative three-dimensional point cloud submaps.
The input image is first divided into regular patches via patch partitioning.
An Image Transformer built with Swin Transformer blocks, patch merging layers, and a fully connected layer extracts multi-scale visual features.
In parallel, the point cloud submaps pass through pooling and a Point Transformer using centroid-aware voxelization and lightweight self-attention.
This produces two-dimensional patch descriptors along with pixel-level positional encodings.
The Point Transformer generates corresponding three-dimensional point descriptors for the submaps.
Concatenating the patch descriptors with positional encodings through a pixel multi-layer perceptron yields fine-grained pixel descriptors.
A NetVLAD layer aggregates the patch descriptors into a compact global image descriptor.
Concatenating patch descriptors and point features into a score multi-layer perceptron with softmax produces patch classification scores.
A second NetVLAD module pools the point descriptors into positive and negative global point cloud descriptors.
Pixel descriptors determine coordinate correspondences, which enter a differentiable Perspective-n-Point solver to estimate the six-degrees-of-freedom camera pose.
A patch classification loss supervises the patch-level matching accuracy.
Finally, the global image and point descriptors are aligned through a global matching loss for retrieval consistency.
The metric learning pipeline begins with diverse anchor mining, selecting pairs of daytime positive and anchor images from a diverse pool.
The anchor image is then fed into a trained generator network that translates the daytime scene into a synthetic night image.
A random skip mechanism allows some daytime anchors to bypass night translation, preserving standard daytime training pairs.
Following translation, hard-negative mining identifies five challenging nighttime images from different scenes whose descriptors are closest to the anchor.
The positive sample, anchor image, and five negative samples are all processed through the embedding network with photometric normalization.
The network extracts global descriptor vectors for the positive image, the anchor, and each of the negative examples.
Finally, contrastive learning optimizes the model by minimizing the Euclidean distance between positive pairs while penalizing negative pairs falling within the margin.
The framework begins with cross-view completion pre-training on pairs of scene images.
Two views of the same scene are provided, with patches in the first image heavily masked.
Both the masked and unmasked views pass through monocular encoders with shared weights to extract visual features.
A binocular decoder then jointly processes features from both views to implicitly reason about scene geometry.
The decoder reconstructs the target image, completing the cross-view pre-training task.
The pre-trained architecture is then finetuned for dense geometric downstream tasks without masking.
For stereo matching, the model takes an unmasked stereo image pair.
The left and right images are independently encoded by the monocular encoders.
The binocular decoder fuses tokens from both views to establish dense spatial correspondences.
This directly produces the disparity map for stereo matching.
Similarly, for optical flow estimation, consecutive temporal frames are fed to the model.
The monocular encoders extract feature tokens for each time frame separately.
The binocular decoder processes the dual feature representations across time.
Yielding the final predicted optical flow field.
In the proxy anonymization training stage, video frames from an action dataset are fed into the training pipeline.
A UNet architecture serves as the anonymizer network, transforming the input frames to remove private visual attributes while preserving action utility.
The anonymized output is guided by a budget network using a contrastive loss to minimize mutual information across frames and obscure personal identity.
Simultaneously, a proxy video encoder is optimized with an action recognition loss that combines cross-entropy classification and a temporally distinct triplet loss.
To formulate the triplet loss, augmented video clips are sampled from both matching and temporally distinct time segments along the video timeline.
In the representation space, embeddings from the same timestamp are brought closer together, while embeddings from distinct timestamps are repelled to promote temporal distinctiveness.
During downstream deployment on surveillance anomaly datasets, raw video feeds are anonymized using the frozen, pre-trained anonymizer network.
The anonymized video feed is then processed by the trained video feature extractor to produce privacy-preserved representation features.
Finally, these anonymized features are provided to a weakly-supervised anomaly detection algorithm to detect anomalous events without risking privacy leakage.
The legend outlines the foundational components, including the autoencoder modules, latent embeddings, noise representations, and network architectures.
The pipeline begins by passing both the character image and the skeleton pose image into a pre-trained encoder.
The encoder outputs a clean latent embedding for the character and an aligned pose latent embedding for the skeleton.
The clean latent then undergoes the forward diffusion process to generate a noisy latent embedding.
The primary UNet backbone receives text conditioning prompts across its cross-attention layers to guide generation.
Rather than using cross-attention, the pose latent is directly concatenated with the noisy latent embedding and fed into the UNet.
The model iteratively denoises the latent representation while maintaining native structural guidance from the skeleton.
Finally, the fully denoised clean latent is decoded to synthesize the output character matching the target pose.
In part a, the heatmap-guided denoising loss evaluates the difference between the ground-truth noise and the estimated noise.
Subtracting the estimated noise directly from the ground truth noise provides the original standard denoising loss.
In parallel, the noise difference is mapped through the decoder to create an image-space difference map.
A pre-trained pose estimator module extracts body joint heatmaps to locate human regions with high synthesis errors.
Applying this heatmap soft mask scales the loss on human areas, which is combined with the original loss to form the total objective.
For comparison, part b illustrates the dual-branch ControlNet approach, which locks the original UNet backbone while adding a trainable branch.
In that design, pose condition features are extracted separately and added back into the frozen branch to produce the estimated noise.
The framework begins with an unlabelled target image to perform free-energy based instance selection.
The target image is processed through the Vision Transformer backbone to extract its attention map.
In parallel, a complementary non-attention map is derived from the non-attended regions.
A non-attention masking operation is then applied to the target image using this mask.
The masked non-attention image patches are subsequently passed through the Vision Transformer.
The model outputs undergo both a prediction consistency test and a free-energy comparison to verify attention quality.
The consistency probability and the free-energy selection indicator are combined via multiplication.
This determines the final instance selection score to guide the pseudo-label self-training loss.
In subfigure b, the score normalizer module receives the classification logits layer output.
The energy normalizer standardizes energy scores to compute the energy normalization loss.
Simultaneously, the free-energy normalizer calculates and standardizes free-energy terms to compute the free-energy loss.
In subfigure c, source and target domain datasets are simultaneously processed through Vision Transformer backbones.
The score alignment module aligns cross-domain features while dedicated score normalization modules regularize both domains.
Finally, the shading image is multiplied with the refined albedo to yield the photorealistic shaded image, which is composited onto the background using the generated mask.
In the target observation space, points are sampled along a camera ray defined by the rendering viewpoint.
A backward warping transformation, guided by a shared skinning weight network, begins mapping the sample out of observation space.
This maps the sampled point into the category-level canonical space, representing a coarse, generic T-pose mesh.
Using the learned skinning weights, forward warping transforms this canonical point into the observation spaces of the support images.
Meanwhile, a sparse set of input video frames captures the subject under different poses and viewpoints.
A shared convolutional image encoder processes each input frame to extract corresponding 2D feature maps.
The forward-warped points are projected into each support view to establish spatial correspondences on the feature maps.
This queries both pixel-aligned local image features and SMPL mesh-guided local features across all input views.
A deformation network then combines the category canonical point with the pixel-aligned features to model fine shape details.
This outputs a point in the instance-level canonical space, capturing subject-specific identity and geometry.
In the rendering network, the instance coordinate embedding is assembled alongside the pixel-aligned and SMPL local features.
Finally, a multi-layer perceptron predicts the volume density and color values for neural rendering of novel views.
A neuromorphic vision sensor observes the real scene containing a human subject.
The camera outputs an asynchronous event stream formatted into voxel grids.
Without protection, an adversary can apply an event-to-image reconstruction network directly to the raw stream.
This reconstructs clear grayscale imagery, exposing sensitive identity information.
To protect privacy, an event anonymization autoencoder scrambles the voxel grid while preserving structural context.
The anonymized event stream is fed directly into a person re-identification backbone to extract feature embeddings.
Simultaneously, an inversion attack attempts to compromise the anonymized stream.
The attacked output is processed by the event-to-image reconstruction network.
The resulting reconstructed image remains heavily degraded and unidentifiable, successfully preserving individual privacy.
The pipeline begins with the editing guidance generation stage to convert user edits into supervision signals.
A pretrained teacher model encapsulates the original neural radiance field of the reconstructed scene.
When a user interactively edits a region, such as scaling an object, a spatial mapping function is established.
Sampled points and ray directions in the edited target space are mapped back to the source space, querying the teacher model to obtain color and density guidance.
This generated guidance is then transferred to a two-stage student training framework designed for instant preview.
Student supervision combines a local loss on the edited object with a global loss over the entire scene.
During local pretraining, only local feature parameters are updated while decoder weights remain frozen, enabling instant preview within one second.
In the second stage, global fine-tuning refines the entire scene network using full supervision from teacher inference.
The resulting student model delivers fully converged, high-fidelity rendering of the edited 3D scene.
The generation process begins in the mapping network, where a Gaussian random noise vector is sampled.
A multi-layer perceptron transforms this noise code into an intermediate latent style vector.
In parallel, extrinsic and intrinsic camera parameters define the viewing rays cast through each pixel.
These rays are converted into a spatial Plücker embedding to parameterize the light field without redundancy.
The synthesis network modulates intermediate feature maps with the style code while concatenating the ray embedding at every layer.
At the initial stage, a coarse feature map is modulated and concatenated with a downsampled ray embedding.
The network progressively upsamples the representation, allowing the generator to associate camera rays with appearance.
As resolution increases across layers, mid-level facial features and geometry emerge.
Fine-scale textures and high-frequency details are refined in the final feature maps.
These features synthesize a high-resolution, viewpoint-conditioned output image.
The discriminator evaluates the generated image conditioned directly on the original camera parameters.
Finally, the discriminator outputs a real or fake prediction to drive adversarial training.
The pipeline begins by taking the input image alongside a spatially augmented positive sample.
A set of negative image samples capturing varied crowd scenes and weather conditions is also gathered.
All image samples are passed into a shared VGG encoder.
The encoder extracts deep image feature representations for the positive, input, and negative samples.
Within the Contrastive Weather-adaptive Module, these features are fed into a weather encoder.
The weather encoder outputs corresponding weight vectors for each branch.
A weather bank maintains learned weather prototypes, regularized by a compact prototype loss.
The weight vectors and the weather bank are combined through matrix multiplication.
This multiplication yields patch-wise weather-adaptive queries across the positive, input, and negative branches.
A contrastive loss optimizes the queries, while the input weather query is forwarded through a multi-layer perceptron.
In the weather-aware crowd counting stage, a transformer decoder takes the weather query along with keys and values from the input features.
The transformer decoder produces weather-aware crowd counting features.
A final decoder processes these crowd counting features.
Finally, the model generates the predicted crowd density map, trained under a Bayesian loss.
First, the input time series data is routed into the Spatial View branch.
Within this branch, it first undergoes task-wise normalization.
This is followed by a task-wise affine transformation.
Simultaneously, the input enters the parallel Temporal View branch.
Here, the features are processed with task-wise normalization,
followed by a shared affine transformation across tasks.
Concurrently, the input is fed into the Original View branch.
It passes through an initial identity mapping,
and a second identity layer to preserve unaltered feature representations.
Finally, the outputs from the spatial, temporal, and original views are concatenated together to form the unified block output.
The pipeline begins with the extraction phase, accessing raw records stored in the data source.
The extracted data is routed to a decoder to parse the raw byte streams into image data.
This produces the decoded base image ready for feature manipulation.
In the transformation stage, parser preprocessing performs data augmentations, including random hue, saturation, and zooming.
The result is a transformed and augmented image sample.
During the loading stage, data loading procedures execute batching, prefetching, and memory caching.
Finally, the processed dataset is streamed directly as input into the model.
The training pipeline begins with the Breast Cancer Image Dataset, providing source data for segmentation and classification workflows.
In the segmentation branch, raw ultrasonography images are extracted from the dataset.
These images enter the preprocessing stage,
where they undergo dimension scaling to 128 by 128 pixels followed by pixel normalization.
Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) then clusters pixels into superpixels to mitigate noise.
The clustered images are fed into a modified U-Net encoder-decoder network alongside ground truth masks.
Completing this training yields the trained segmentation model.
In parallel, masked images and corresponding class labels are retrieved for detection training.
A pre-trained VGG 16 model extracts deep spatial features from these masked ultrasound images.
Extracted features are processed through five fully connected dense layers with dropout and activations.
This establishes the trained detection model for classifying tumor types.
Finally, the trained components combine into the unified breast cancer detection pipelining framework.
The pipeline begins with a sequence of five hundred twelve dimensional input feature vectors.
These vectors are organized into an input feature matrix labeled F sub w, with dimensions five hundred twelve by n.
Inside the scaled dot product attention sub-block, the matrix branches through fully connected layers into key transpose, query, and value matrices.
The key transpose and query representations are multiplied together and processed by a softmax function.
This yields an n-by-n matrix of self-attention weights labeled W sub s a.
The self-attention weights are then multiplied with the value matrix.
The result feeds into the cross-walk attention sub-block as an intermediate matrix labeled H sub a.
A per-row softmax operation is then applied across the matrix columns.
Next, the softmax output is combined element-wise with a bypass connection from the original matrix F sub w.
This creates the cross-walk attention matrix labeled G, with dimensions five hundred twelve by n.
The column vectors are then aggregated through a summation operation.
Finally, the system outputs the five hundred twelve dimensional feature vector labeled f sub a.
The legend outlines the core modules, including SSFT, SFT, residual blocks, and convolutional layers.
The pipeline begins with a blurred face image as input.
Within the deblurring stream, the input image enters the encoder through an initial convolution layer labeled E zero.
The first encoder stage processes feature maps through residual blocks followed by a downsampling convolution.
A second stage further extracts features and downsamples the spatial resolution.
The encoder concludes at bottleneck stage E four to form compact feature representations.
Features from each intermediate encoder stage branch into the prior estimation stream via SSFT modules and residual blocks.
This stream outputs multi-scale estimated priors labeled P-hat one, P-hat two, and P-hat three.
In the decoder, stage D three modulates bottleneck features with estimated prior P-hat three using an SFT module.
Decoder stage D two incorporates estimated prior P-hat two and continues upsampling.
Stage D one modulates with prior P-hat one, combining the decoded features with a skip connection from E zero.
A final convolution block labeled D zero maps the merged representations.
This generates the predicted deblurred image, presented alongside the target ground truth image.
A fixed VGG Face model extracts multi-scale feature priors labeled P one, P two, and P three from the target image.
Prior loss supervises the estimated priors against target features, while pixel loss compares the predicted image to the ground truth.
Finally, a discriminator evaluates sets of estimated and real feature priors to compute the adversarial loss.
The architecture is organized into local and global attention pathways across channel and spatial attention stages, culminating in a fusion module.
The input feature tensor enters the network and branches into both the local and global processing pathways.
In the channel attention stage, both local and global channel attention maps are computed.
The local channel attention map scales the feature stream followed by a residual addition, producing the local channel feature tensor.
Simultaneously, the global channel attention map modulates the input stream to produce the global channel feature tensor.
Next, in the spatial attention stage, separate local and global spatial attention maps are derived.
The local spatial attention map is applied with a residual connection, generating the refined local feature tensor.
Concurrently, the global spatial attention map is applied with a residual addition to output the refined global feature tensor.
In the fusion module, the local features, direct bypass features, and global features are weighted by distinct parameters and summed together.
This produces the final fused output tensor, combining both local and global contextual information.
The pipeline takes K-shot support images and a query image as inputs, referencing the aggregation, tensor shape, and path notations shown in the legend.

The memory architecture is divided into User Space and Kernel Space.
In User Space, execution begins at the Database Process.
The process initiates an asynchronous write call.
This is followed by a synchronous fsync operation.
The write call routes into the Page Cache within Kernel Space and returns immediately, creating dirty pages.
The Kernel Flusher Thread periodically handles writebacks from the Page Cache.
Requests pass into the I/O Queue, while fsync waits for disk completion.
At the bottom is Persistent Storage, containing the Block Device.
Finally, enqueued operations are flushed from the I/O Queue down to the Block Device.

The initializing process begins with a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model with frozen parameters.
The model is passed into the Frequency Guided Densification module.
Frequency Guided Densification is structured into two main phases shown below.
In Phase 1, the contribution of each 3D Gaussian to rendering quality is evaluated.
Low-contribution 3D Gaussians are removed.
In Phase 2, views are rendered from multiple perspectives.
Each rendered image is split into a grid of patches.
A Discrete Fourier Transform is applied to the patches.
This converts the image patches into transformed frequency representations.
Transformed patches enter the high frequency detection stage.
Each transformed patch is combined via Hadamard product with a quadratic mask.
The quadratic mask highlights high frequency regions.
Patches exhibiting high frequency components are selected.
The 3D Gaussians within these high frequency areas are split into denser elements.
This yields the updated 3D Gaussian Splatting representation after densification.
A gradient mask is constructed across the Gaussian parameter set.
In the fine-tuning process, parameters are unfrozen for model optimization.
Rendering is performed using the fine-tuned 3D Gaussians.
A Discrete Wavelet Transform decomposes the rendered image into frequency sub-bands.
The low frequency component is routed forward.
A pre-trained decoder with frozen parameters processes the low frequency signal.
The decoder outputs the recovered decoded message.
Meanwhile, the high frequency components from the rendered image are extracted.
The ground truth image is introduced for supervision.
A Discrete Wavelet Transform is applied to the ground truth image.
This isolates the high frequency components of the ground truth.
Reconstruction and perceptual loss functions compare rendered views with ground truth.
A wavelet loss is computed between rendered and ground truth high frequencies.
A fixed message serves as target supervision.
Message loss compares the decoded message with the fixed message.
All objectives combine into a single total loss function.
The total loss guides the optimizer.
Finally, the optimizer applies the gradient mask via Hadamard product to update the fine-tuned 3D Gaussians.

A 3D indoor scene is modeled compositionally from multi-view inputs.

Along each ray, multiple 3D spatial points are sampled.
For each queried point coordinate,

The network outputs a vector containing signed distance function values for each individual object.
These encompass specific instance geometries, such as pillows,
lamps,

extracting the global scene signed distance value,
denoted as the overall scene SDF.
Next, the occlusion-aware object opacity module calculates individual object opacities.
Object SDFs are first converted into individual object density distributions.
Concurrently, the global scene transmittance is computed along the ray,
and multiplied by each object's density.
This produces occlusion-aware object opacities that account for frontal blocking.
The composite weight function governs the overall volume rendering contribution.
An object opacity loss is evaluated,
supervising the rendered object opacities directly against 2D instance segmentation masks.
Finally, several regularization and multi-modal rendering losses are optimized.
An Eikonal loss enforces valid distance field gradients across the scene.
An object distinction regularization loss prevents internal collision and overlap between separate instances.
Volume rendering synthesizes geometric cues and appearance.
A scale-invariant depth loss,
supervises rendered depth maps.
A surface normal loss,
aligns predicted surface normals with pseudo-ground-truth,
derived from a pre-trained monocular estimation network.

ensures photorealistic rendering against ground truth captured images.

Given an input crowd image, the Point Query Transformer pipeline begins by extracting visual representations.
A standard CNN backbone processes the input image to extract deep feature representations.
This produces a feature map F, where each spatial element is treated as an individual token.
The feature tokens are passed into a transformer encoder utilizing progressive rectangle-window attention.
Initial encoder layers compute self-attention within large horizontal rectangular windows to capture contextual crowd information.
Subsequent encoder layers progressively reduce the rectangle window size to focus on local regional details efficiently.
The encoder outputs context-enriched image feature representations for the decoding stage.
In parallel, a uniform grid of sparse querying points is initialized across the image canvas.
A region-based quadtree splitter evaluates local image features to determine whether a region is dense or sparse.
Points in dense regions are dynamically split into four sub-points, whereas points in sparse regions remain undivided.
This adaptive quadtree splitting generates denser point queries precisely where high crowd congestion occurs.
The resulting candidate points are paired with sampled CNN features and positional embeddings to form point queries.
In the object querying stage, the transformer decoder decodes sparse queries inside local rectangular windows.
Dense queries are progressively decoded in smaller local windows, modeling relationships guided by image context.
The decoded point queries gather both semantic crowd context and spatial localization information.
These decoded queries are passed in parallel into the multi-layer perceptron prediction head.
For each query, the head predicts a person classification probability along with precise coordinate offsets.
Surplus split queries that land on background regions are classified as containing no person.
Likewise, sparse queries covering empty areas correctly output no-person predictions.
Queries in dense regions successfully detect individual heads with high probability and localized offsets.
The individual point predictions are collected and mapped back onto the original image space.
This yields the final crowd count and precise instance-level localizations across both sparse and congested scenes.

Looking closer at the base Transformer Block design:
The input passes through batch normalization.
Pixel-wise and depth-wise convolutions generate queries,
which are reshaped into attention tokens.
Parallel convolutions produce keys,
which are reshaped accordingly.
Similarly, the value projections are generated,
and reshaped.
The queries and keys are multiplied via dot product,
normalized by Softmax across channels,
and applied to the values.
After reshaping back to spatial dimensions,
a pixel-wise convolution projects the attention output,
which is added to the shortcut connection.
The result is processed by the Gated Feed Forward Network.
Inside the Gated Feed Forward Network:
Batch normalization normalizes incoming activations into two parallel paths.
The upper path uses a pixel-wise convolution
followed by Sigmoid activation to create a gating mask.
The lower branch applies pixel-wise and depth-wise convolutions to strengthen locality.
Both paths are element-wise multiplied to gate the feature flow,
and added back to the residual input for the final output.

Within the MCP Tool Collection, the pipeline identifies the correct tools.
Distractor tools are also introduced into the collection.
Together, these tools combine to form the Candidate Tool List.
In parallel, the Task Set supplies a set of real-world tasks.
Both the candidate tools and real-world tasks are fed into the AutoGen-based Sandbox.
The sandbox handles dynamic MCP tool loading,
manages local MCP servers,
and provides stable and reproducible execution.
The sandbox communicates with the LLM-based Agent via tool calls and execution feedback.
Within the agent, processing begins with task understanding,
proceeds to tool selection,
and concludes with parameter generation.
Outputs are then routed to the Evaluation and Scoring stage.
Performance is measured across correct tool selection,
anti-interference robustness,
task completion,
and efficiency metrics.
